overview: This section builds a fully scalable WordPress site (MyWordPress.com) that must serve picture uploads and keep user data and blog content in MySQL. It walks through the database layer (RDS Multi-AZ, then Aurora Multi-AZ with Read Replicas) and then the storage decision for uploaded images: an EBS volume attached to one instance versus EFS shared across the Auto Scaling group's instances in multiple Availability Zones. The exam tests this as the canonical "stateful app needs shared storage" scenario: recognise the EBS single-instance limitation and pick EFS for a distributed multi-AZ application.

coreConcepts.definition: A WordPress deployment in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones, with content in MySQL and images on shared storage, so any instance can serve any user.
An application that keeps data or files on its instances (such as uploaded images), which conflicts with a stateless fleet behind Auto Scaling and a load balancer.
The web tier: EC2 instances launched across Availability Zones 1, 2 and 3 that scale on demand and receive traffic from a load balancer.
The database layer for user data and blog content, deployed as RDS Multi-AZ so a standby in another AZ takes over if the primary fails.
A synchronous standby replica in a second Availability Zone, used for failover / high availability, not for scaling reads.
Aurora keeps the same data in multiple AZs and provides easy Multi-AZ high availability without you managing replication.
Additional Aurora read endpoints that offload read traffic and improve read scaling; the section pairs them with Multi-AZ for scaling the database layer.
Images are written to an Amazon EBS volume attached to the instance; EBS is block storage tied to a single instance (and a single AZ).
A block-storage volume attached to one EC2 instance; it exists in one Availability Zone and cannot be shared by instances in other AZs.
With an EBS volume, an image uploaded to instance A is invisible to instance B, so users hitting another instance in the Auto Scaling group see broken images.

coreConcepts.term: EBS vs EFS for distributed apps
coreConcepts.definition: EBS suits a single-instance application; EFS is a shared file system for distributed applications whose instances span AZs.
Uploaded images go to Amazon EFS, which is mounted by every instance, so any instance in any AZ can display any uploaded image.
Each instance mounts EFS through an elastic network interface (ENI) in its own Availability Zone, giving all instances one shared file system.
A managed, shared file system that multiple EC2 instances across Availability Zones can mount at the same time — the fix for distributed upload storage.
EBS provides block storage attached to one instance; EFS provides a shared network file system mounted by many instances, which is why EFS fits the distributed case.

mustRemember: EBS is attached to a single instance and lives in one Availability Zone — the canonical reason it fails for a multi-AZ Auto Scaling image-upload design.
EFS is the shared file system: every instance mounts it (each via an ENI in its own AZ), so any instance can serve any uploaded image.
The section's rule: EBS = single-instance application; EFS = distributed application.
RDS MySQL Multi-AZ provides a high-availability standby in a second AZ for failover — not a read-scaling mechanism.
Aurora gives Multi-AZ easily and adds Read Replicas — use it when the database must both survive AZ failure and scale reads.
The architecture spans an Auto Scaling group over Availability Zones 1, 2 and 3, an Elastic Load Balancer in front, and a multi-AZ database behind.
User data and blog content belong in the MySQL-compatible database (RDS MySQL or Aurora MySQL); images belong in EBS (single instance) or EFS (distributed).

keyComparisons.items: EBS vs EFS for uploaded images
keyComparisons.difference: EBS is a block volume attached to one instance in one AZ, so other instances can't see the upload; EFS is a shared file system mounted by all instances across AZs.

keyComparisons.items: EBS single-instance vs distributed Auto Scaling application
keyComparisons.difference: If the app runs on one instance, EBS works; once an Auto Scaling group spreads instances across AZs, the images must live on EFS.

keyComparisons.items: RDS MySQL Multi-AZ vs Aurora with Multi-AZ and Read Replicas
keyComparisons.difference: RDS Multi-AZ gives a synchronous standby for failover only; Aurora adds easy Multi-AZ plus Read Replicas for read scaling.
Multi-AZ is for high availability / failover; Read Replicas are for offloading reads and read scaling.
Block storage attaches to a single instance; file storage is mountable by many instances simultaneously, which is what a distributed app needs.

commonMisunderstandings: EBS is not shared storage: an EBS volume cannot be mounted by instances in different Availability Zones, so it cannot back a multi-AZ Auto Scaling image upload.
Multi-AZ is not for read scaling: the standby is for failover; read scaling needs Read Replicas (Aurora Read Replicas in this section).
Adding more instances does not fix the image problem — without EFS, each new instance has its own EBS volume and misses previously uploaded images.
EFS does not require all instances in one AZ: instances in different AZs each mount the shared file system through an ENI.
mentalModels: Think of EBS as a USB drive plugged into one server — only that server sees the file.
Think of EFS as a shared network drive every server in every AZ can mount — uploads follow the user to any instance.
Think of Multi-AZ as the spare tire (failover) and Read Replicas as extra lanes (read throughput).
edgeCases: If the application is genuinely single-instance, EBS for images is acceptable; the problem appears only when Auto Scaling distributes instances across AZs.
The database layer can be either RDS MySQL Multi-AZ or Aurora MySQL Multi-AZ with Read Replicas — the storage decision for images is independent of that choice.
WordPress needs a writable shared location for uploads; EFS provides it for every instance behind the load balancer.

whenToUse.situation: Uploaded images must be visible to any EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling group spanning multiple AZs
whenToUse.use: Amazon EFS mounted by every instance

whenToUse.situation: Application runs on a single EC2 instance and stores files locally
MySQL database must survive an AZ failure
whenToUse.use: RDS MySQL Multi-AZ or Aurora Multi-AZ

whenToUse.situation: Database must also serve heavy read traffic
Need a fully scalable WordPress site with user data, blog content and images
whenToUse.use: ALB + Auto Scaling group across AZs + multi-AZ MySQL database + EFS for images

patternsToRecognize.signal: "Users sometimes see broken or missing images after new instances launch"
patternsToRecognize.indicates: Images stored on EBS instead of a shared file system — move to EFS

patternsToRecognize.signal: "Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones storing user uploads"
patternsToRecognize.indicates: EFS is the expected answer; EBS is the distractor

patternsToRecognize.signal: "Database must be highly available and handle read-heavy traffic"
"High availability with automatic failover to another AZ"

examTraps.trap: "Use an EBS volume for uploads because it's attached to the instance and fast"
examTraps.correction: EBS is single-instance and single-AZ; instances elsewhere in the Auto Scaling group cannot see those images. Use EFS for the distributed case.
The Multi-AZ standby is for failover only; read scaling comes from Read Replicas.

examTraps.trap: "Attach the same EBS volume to instances in all AZs"
examTraps.correction: That is the EFS pattern; EBS volumes cannot be shared across Availability Zones.

examTraps.trap: "Aurora Multi-AZ makes Read Replicas unnecessary for scaling reads"
examTraps.correction: Multi-AZ addresses availability; Read Replicas address read scaling — the section uses both.

beyondSource: EFS is a Regional, multi-AZ file system with mount targets per AZ; instances mount it over NFS through those targets.
EBS volumes are AZ-scoped and replicated within that AZ; multi-attach io1/io2 volumes are limited to the same AZ and are not a substitute for EFS.
Amazon S3 is a common alternative for WordPress media in a stateless design, but this section's comparison is EBS vs EFS.
